The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI∗ Alexander Bick Adam Blandin Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis & CEPR Vanderbilt University David J. Deming Harvard Kennedy School & NBER October 27, 2025 Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a potentially important new technology, but its impact on the economy depends on the speed and intensity of adoption. This paper reports results from a series of nationally representative U.S. surveys of generative AI use at work and at home. As of late 2024, 45% of the U.S. population age 18-64 uses generative AI. Among employed respondents, 27% used generative AI for work at least once in the previous week: 10% used it every workday, and 17% on some but not all workdays. Relative to each technology’s first mass-market product launch, work adoption of generative AI has been as fast as the personal computer (PC), and overall adoption has been faster than either PCs or the internet. Between 1 and 7% of all work hours are currently assisted by generative AI, and respondents report time savings equivalent to 1.4% of total work hours. Potential productivity gains vary widely by industry, and firm climate and policies play an important role in adoption patterns. 1 Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) has quickly emerged as a potentially important work- place technology. The large language model ChatGPT debuted in November 2022 and, by December 2024, had over 300 million weekly users. Several studies find that genAI boosts pro- ductivity in specific cases (Brynjolfsson et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2024; Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Demirci et al., 2025; Dillon et al., 2025; Kanazawa et al., 2025; Noy and Zhang, 2023; Otis et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2023), and some project genAI will have large macroeconomic effects (Chui et al., 2023; Filippucci et al., 2024). Yet others predict only modest aggregate impacts (Acemoglu, 2024). These differing views largely reflect uncertainty about the extent of genAI adoption today and in the future.1 This paper studies the adoption of genAI using data from the first nationally representa- tive U.S. surveys of genAI usage at work and at home. Our data come from the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS), a national online labor market survey of working age adults aged 18-64 that has run since 2020 (Bick and Blandin, 2023). We report the combined results of two surveys fielded in August and November 2024, which collectively included more than 10,000 respondents. These surveys include questions about genAI adoption that we adapt from the Current Population Survey’s Computer and Internet Supplement (CIU), which was introduced in 1984 to document computer (and later, internet) adoption. We also introduce novel ques- tions to measure how intensively individuals use the technology, which tasks genAI assists with, how much time it saves them, and workplace barriers or support for adoption. The resulting microdata will be made publicly available, addressing calls for more research that develops and shares novel data (Ethiraj et al., 2019). We use this data to address three main questions. First, how many individuals are currently using genAI? Pooling our August and November 2024 surveys, 32% of workers reported using genAI for work: 10% used it every work day, 17% on some but not all work days, and 5% did not use it in the previous week. One third of respondents report using genAI outside of work. Overall, 45% of respondents report using genAI either for work or outside of work. The most commonly used products are ChatGPT (32% of all respondents), Gemini (19%) and embedded products such as Microsoft Copilot (15%). To benchmark these results, we show that the rate of workplace genAI adoption in 2024, two years after the release of ChatGPT, is similar to the rate of workplace computer adoption in 1 Acemoglu et al. (2022) analyze online job vacancies related to AI, but their data predates ChatGPT. Albanesi et al. (2024), Eisfeldt et al. (2024), and Gathmann et al. (2024) compare occupations according to predictions of AI exposure but do not have data on actual adoption. Humlum and Vestergaard (2025) find no meaningful impacts of genAI adoption on employment and earnings in Denmark among workers in 11 occupations that are particularly exposed to genAI. 1

1984, three years after the release of the IBM PC (the first mass-market computer). The com- puter and related information technologies induced far-reaching changes in firm organization and management, which led to substantial productivity gains (Brynjolfsson and Hitt, 1996). The similar pace of genAI adoption thus far suggests that it has the potential to be similarly disruptive. Moreover, we show that genAI adoption by workers is proceeding at a faster pace than adoption by firms, highlighting both challenges and opportunities for managers seeking to capitalize on this new technology (Babina et al., 2024; Bonney et al., 2024; Doshi and Moore, 2025; McElheran et al., 2024).2 Second, which workers are currently using genAI, and what factors contribute to an individ- ual’s adoption decision? We find substantial variation in genAI adoption across demographic and labor market characteristics. Adoption has been faster for male, younger, more educated, and higher-wage workers. Adoption also differs greatly by occupation, suggesting that differ- ences in job roles and responsibilities are an important determinant of adoption. Consistent with this, we show that recent estimates of genAI task-based exposure are highly predictive of actual adoption (Eloundou et al., 2024; Felten et al., 2021), and that occupations with lower adoption also have higher shares of workers who report that genAI is not useful for their job. These findings contribute to our understanding of how genAI maps onto specific tasks and roles within the firm, which is relevant both for allocating adoption support and adapting firm organization. We provide evidence that firm climate and policies also appear to play an important role in workers’ adoption choice. A sizable share of workers who do not use genAI cite workplace barriers as a key reason, and this share is particularly large in a few occupations who may deal with sensitive data. Alternatively, workers whose employers encourage them to use genAI are much more likely to do so, even after controlling for other characteristics. This suggests that when job tasks are amenable to genAI adoption, firms can play an active role by promoting usage, offering training, and removing organizational barriers to adoption. Third, how large are potential productivity gains from genAI? Based on self-reported time savings due to genAI, the average genAI user would need to work 5.2% more hours in order to complete their work without genAI, implying 1.4% time savings across all workers (including non-users). We use a standard production model to estimate potential productivity gains at the industry and aggregate level. We find wide variation in potential productivity gains by industry, 2 The Census BTOS Survey estimates between August and November 2024 5.4% of firms had incorporated AI technologies into their production process. This suggests that firm-based measures may miss an important share of genAI adoption. Aaron Levie, the founder and CEO of Box, a cloud storage provider, compares this pattern with past technologies: “It’s almost a one-to-one parallel with the early wave of consumerization of IT. We saw that exact same dynamic in the early 2010s, which was employees of enterprises were pretty frustrated with their traditional document management and collaboration technology, and so they would go out and just go onto a web browser, sign up for a Box account, and then bring it into their organization.” (Levine, 2024) 2

driven by differences in both the intensity of genAI use and labor cost shares. These factors can offset one another: for example, the information services sector has high rates of genAI use and time savings, but its estimated productivity gain is muted by its low labor cost share. At the aggregate level, we estimate a potential productivity gain of 1.2% based on current genAI use. This is close to Acemoglu (2024), who uses a similar framework to estimate a 0.7% gain based on predicted task exposure rather than actual adoption. Notably, however, Acemoglu (2024) assumed these productivity gains may take a decade to materialize. In contrast, our estimates reflect current adoption and time savings, implying a faster pace of diffusion. We also emphasize that our estimates do not capture potential productivity gains from using genAI to reorganize or completely automate production processes, and therefore likely represent a lower bound over longer horizons (Bresnahan and Trajtenberg, 1995; Brynjolfsson and Hitt, 2000; David, 1990; Jovanovic and Rousseau, 2005). 2 Data Sources and Measurement 2.1 The Real-Time Population Survey (RPS) Our main data source is the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS), a national labor market survey of U.S. adults aged 18-64 (for a detailed discussion, see Bick and Blandin 2023). The RPS is fielded online by Qualtrics, a large commercial survey provider, and has collected multiple survey waves each year starting in 2020. The RPS is designed to mirror the Current Population Survey (CPS) along key dimensions. The RPS matches questions on demographics and labor market outcomes in the basic CPS and CPS Outgoing Rotation Group, using the same word-for-word phrasing when practical and replicating the intricate sequence of questions necessary to elicit labor market outcomes in a manner consistent with the CPS (US Census Bureau, 2015). Replicating key portions of an existing high-quality survey ensures that survey concepts are comparable, which allows researchers to validate RPS outcomes against a widely used benchmark with a larger sample size and to construct sample weights. Bick and Blandin (2023) and Bick et al. (2025a,b) show that the RPS closely aligns with government household surveys on distributions of employment, hours worked, earnings, industry composition, employee tenure, and work from home. In June 2024, the RPS introduced a novel module measuring genAI use both at work and at home. 3

2.1.1 RPS Sample Qualtrics panel members are recruited to the panel online and, in our case, can participate in exchange for 30 to 50 percent of the $5.50 paid per completed survey. The Qualtrics panel includes about 15 million members and is not a random sample of the U.S. population. However, Qualtrics can target survey invitations to specific demographic groups. The RPS sample was designed to be nationally representative across key demographics. We also include measures to filter out low quality responses. Details on sampling and data quality procedures can be found in Appendix A.1. We fielded the RPS with a pilot genAI module in June 2024 and received 2,551 responses. We then launched the full genAI module with the August and November 2024 waves and received 5,014 and 5,329 responses respectively. All surveys started fielding during the same weeks that the CPS conducted its corresponding surveys. Because the results are very similar across all surveys but our June pilot featured fewer questions, we report results from the pooled August and November surveys. Appendix B replicates the main figures of the paper separately by survey waves. Appendix Table A.1 compares the unweighted sample composition between the CPS and RPS along the demographics targeted in the sampling procedure for our main surveys (columns 1 and 2). The bottom panel also compares employment status in the CPS and RPS, which was not targeted in the sampling procedure. The two surveys yield very similar population shares. 2.1.2 Sample Weights and Validation To address remaining discrepancies, we construct sample weights using the raking algorithm of Deming and Stephan (1940), ensuring that the weighted sample proportions align with the demographic characteristics targeted in the sampling procedure and that the employment shares in the RPS align with the CPS as well. Details on weighting can be found in Appendix A.2.3 In Appendix A.3, we show that the distribution of usual weekly earnings, occupation, and industry shares in the RPS, which were not targeted during sampling, closely align with the CPS, in both the raw and weighted data. 3 In particular, Appendix A.2.1 discusses a weighting adjustment we applied based on an experimental survey which randomized the sequencing of questions in the genAI module. 4

2.2 Measurement of Generative AI Use When designing our survey, a key goal was to enable comparisons to the historical adoption of other technologies. To facilitate these comparisons, we use existing technology adoption questions from the CPS Computer and Internet Use supplement (CIU) as a template for our own questions regarding genAI. In the CIU, the leading question about computer adoption at work for employed respondents was: Do you [directly] use a computer for your job? (No/Yes) A second question asks about computer use at home: Do you [directly] use a computer at home? (No/Yes) These questions were asked in 1984, 1989, 1993, 1997, 2001, and 2003, with the word “directly” being omitted in the last two years.4 The RPS genAI module begins with a definition of genAI: Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that creates text, images, audio, or video in response to prompts. Some examples of Generative AI include ChatGPT, Gemini, and Midjourney. We included examples of popular genAI products because we thought some respondents may be more familiar with those product names than with the broader concept of genAI. After defining genAI, the module asks respondents whether they had heard of the concept prior to the survey. Overall, 88.4% reported having heard of genAI; the remaining 11.6% who answered “No” skip the remainder of the module. Respondents who answer “Yes” continue with the survey. For employed respondents, the next question asks about genAI use at work: Do you use Generative AI for your job? (No/Yes) This question is designed to mirror the analogous computer use question from the CIU, discussed above. We opted for the version asked from 2001 onwards that omitted the word “directly.” Another question later in the survey asks about genAI usage outside work: Do you use Generative AI [outside your job]? (No/Yes) 4 Starting in 2001, the CIU also asked about internet usage. 5

Non-employed respondents are not shown the term in brackets. While the CIU asks about computer use “at home”, we use slightly different language to account for respondents who use genAI on mobile devices outside of their home. The survey asks several follow-up questions of genAI users regarding which products they used, how intensively they used it, and how much time they saved, always distinguishing between work and non-work use. An important caveat regarding our measurement approach is that it will only capture genAI use that respondents are aware of. For example, while typing prompts into ChatGPT is an obvious case of using genAI, automatic AI-assisted writing suggestions are a more subtle case that respondents may not consider. Because our estimates may not detect some passive or embedded uses of the technology, we interpret our estimates a lower bound on the extent of genAI adoption. 3 How Prevalent is Generative AI Use? We presented genAI users a list of common products (and a write-in option) and asked them to select (all) the products they use. This allows us to compare ChatGPT use in the RPS with other surveys. The three most used genAI products were ChatGPT (32% of all respondents), Gemini (19%), and embedded tools like Microsoft Copilot (15%). Appendix Figure C.2a shows the full distribution of product usage. In April 2024, Fletcher and Nielsen (2024) conducted an online survey of ChatGPT adoption using a different survey provider (YouGov). They found that 18% of U.S. adults used ChatGPT at least weekly, compared to 22% who used ChatGPT in the previous week in our Fall 2024 surveys.6 A potential concern with online-based surveys is that they may suffer from selection based on unobservable characteristics that are correlated with genAI use. For example, online survey respondents may be more comfortable using technology and therefore be more likely to use genAI than the overall U.S. population. From this perspective, a valuable point of comparison is a survey conducted by the Pew Research Center (McClain, 2024). That survey sampled respondents using a nationally representative sample of U.S. Postal Services addresses. Im- portantly, the survey included respondents without internet access. (Internet access per se is unlikely to substantially impact our results: in the 2022 ACS, 96.8% of individuals aged 18-64 reported having access to the internet.) They find that in February 2024, 27% of U.S. adults age 18-64 reported ever having used ChatGPT, compared to 32% of individuals who report using ChatGPT in our survey in August and November 2024. Finally, we can also compare genAI adoption by workers to adoption by firms. The monthly Census BTOS Survey asks firms: “In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial In- telligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)” (Bonney et al., 2024). Between August and November 2024, 5.3% of firms report using AI, compared with 32.1% of workers who report using genAI in the RPS. While differences in question wording may explain part of this gap, they are unlikely to account for all of it.7 We conclude that, so far, genAI adoption by workers is outpacing firm-wide adoption, implying that firm-based measures may miss an important share of genAI’s impact (Babina et al., 2024). 3.2 How Does Early Generative AI Adoption Compare to Other Technologies? A key question is whether genAI’s faster adoption was driven by work or non-work use.10 The faster overall pace of genAI adoption compared with PCs is driven by non-work adoption. The middle pair of bars in Figure 2 plots work adoption of genAI and PCs. We find similar work adoption rates for genAI after two years (32%) and PCs after three years (25%). By contrast, the bottom pair of bars in Figure 2 reveals much higher non-work adoption rates for genAI (38%) compared with PCs (5%). The computer and related information technologies induced far-reaching changes in firm organization and management, which led to substantial productivity gains (Brynjolfsson and Hitt, 1996). The similar pace of genAI adoption by workers thus far suggests that this new technology could also be transformative for firms. At the same time, the choice of whether to adopt a technology depends on both its benefits and costs. PCs required purchasing expensive immobile hardware and nontrivial training. In contrast, many genAI products are free or inexpensive and user-friendly. On the one hand, this lower adoption cost likely contributes to genAI’s rapid uptake. On the other hand, this means that similar adoption rates for PCs and genAI at work do not necessarily imply equivalent benefits. 4 Which Workers Use Generative AI? In this section, we document that early genAI adoption has not been uniform throughout the workforce. Understanding which workers are adopting genAI at higher rates provides several important insights. First, because many workers are adopting genAI ahead of firm-level adoption, variation in genAI use can help managers allocate support, training, and integration efforts. Second, we show that employer encouragement of genAI use is highly predictive of adoption, suggesting that firms and managers can influence the nature and extent of genAI use in their organization. Third, adoption patterns shed light on how genAI maps onto specific tasks and roles within the firm, which is relevant for decisions regarding job redesign and firm reorganization. Figure 3 documents demographic heterogeneity in work adoption of genAI. The top panel shows genAI adoption is 6 percentage points higher for men. The middle panel show genAI adoption by age. Workers aged 18-49 have similar adoption rates, while adoption is lower for workers aged 50-64. The bottom panel shows that adoption rates are increasing in educational attainment. In particular, workers with a Bachelor’s degree or more use genAI at roughly twice the rate of non-college educated workers. Differences between demographic groups are primarily driven by users who use genAI every workday or at least once in the previous week. To better understand the relationship between technology use and earnings, we regress earnings, wages, and hours on indicators of the frequency of genAI use while also controlling for occupation, industry, education, and demographic characteristics.11 The results are displayed in Figure 4b. On average, genAI use is associated with a weekly earnings premium of 20 log points, a wage premium of 15 log points, and 5 log points for weekly hours. However, these average effects mask important heterogeneity. The coefficients on earnings, wages, and hours are all increasing in genAI use intensity, and infrequent users show no statistical difference between non-users. Higher wages by (more intensive) users could reflect several factors. First, within an occu- pation and industry jobs that benefit more from genAI may be associated with higher wages (Deming and Kahn, 2018). Second, more productive workers may adopt new technologies more 11 The control variables used in these regressions are indicators for: female, age 18-29, age 40-49, age 50-54, a bachelor’s degree, a graduate degree, Black, Hispanic, occupation group, and industry. 12

rapidly (Nelson and Phelps, 1966). Third, genAI may directly increase workers’ productivity and wages. Our data do not allow us to distinguish between these explanations. 4.1 Tasks, Predicted Exposure, and Generative AI Adoption Why do some groups of workers adopt genAI at higher rates than others? One reason could be that workers differ in their job tasks or responsibilities, and genAI is more helpful in assisting some tasks than others. Consistent with this explanation, we first document that genAI adoption differs greatly between occupations; see Figure 5. The three occupations with the highest genAI adoption are computer and mathematical, management, and business and finance occupations (54%, 52%, and 48%, respectively) and the bottom three are blue collar, office and administration, and personal services occupations (26%, 23%, and 16%, respectively). At the same time, genAI adoption exceeds 20% in all but one occupation groups, suggesting that the technology is useful for a broad range of occupations. As with demographic differences, differences between occupations are driven by the rates of daily and weekly genAI users. Do different adoption rates between occupations reflect differences in tasks or responsibili- ties? One approach to assess this is to construct task-based-exposure measures across occupa- tions (Eloundou et al., 2024; Felten et al., 2021; Webb, 2020). For example, Eloundou et al. (2024) constructs a rubric that assigns each task in the O*NET database a zero or one corre- sponding to whether LLMs (a popular class of genAI) could feasibly produce large productivity gains for that task. They then construct a predicted exposure score for each occupation by aggregating task-level scores for each occupation. Using RPS data, we can ask whether these predictions are correlated with adoption. Our study is the first to evaluate these task-based “exposure” predictions using actual genAI adoption rates.12 Figure 6a plots an occupation group’s predicted genAI exposure from Eloundou et al. (2024) against actual genAI adoption in the 2024 RPS. We find that predicted genAI exposure is highly correlated with actual genAI adoption (ρ = 0.65). In Figure 6b, we find a similar correlation (ρ = 0.71) using the predicted exposure score from Felten et al. (2021). For example, personal service and blue-collar occupations have relatively low predicted exposure and also relatively low adoption, while computer and mathematical occupations have both high predicted exposure and high adoption. The high correlation between predicted exposure and actual adoption provides partial vali- dation of task-based exposure predictions, supporting their utility for researchers. For example, while managers have similar predicted exposure than administrative occupations, many more admin- istrative workers report that genAI is not useful for their job. Another potential reason that task-based exposure predictions may not perfectly predict adoption is that some jobs may face various barriers to adoption. In our question about why workers did not adopt genAI, a second set of explanations relates to adoption barriers: “My employer does not allow me to use genAI; I am unsure whether my employer allows me to use genAI; I feel pressure from coworkers to not use genAI; I have privacy or security concerns; I am unsure how to use genAI for my job.” We define the share of an occupation who does not use genAI because of adoption barriers as the share of all workers in that occupation who ranked at least one of these options in their top two reasons for not using genAI. New technologies raise productivity by enabling complementary innovations in processes, skills, and organizational practices. These innovations typically evolve gradually over time (Brynjolf- 18

To gain early insights into potential productivity gains from genAI, this section documents worker-reported time savings and shows how this data can inform estimates of aggregate and industry/firm-level productivity gains. 5.1 How Much Do Workers Use Generative AI? We begin by documenting sizable variation in the intensity of genAI use among workers. This is important because, as we show in the next section, workers who use genAI more intensively tend to experience greater time savings. Figure 8a reports how much time genAI users spent using the technology in a given day. Specifically, we ask “Please think back to the days LAST WEEK on which you used Generative AI at work. On average, how much time did you spend actively using Generative AI at work? ” Respondents could select from three options: 15 minutes or less per day, between 15 minutes and one hour per day, or more than an hour per day.13 Figure 8a shows that 36.9% of genAI users report using genAI for an hour or more per day at work, 42.8% used it for between 15 and 60 minutes per day, and 20.3% used it for less than 15 minutes per day. Frequency and intensity of genAI use are positively correlated. 65.7% of daily genAI users report using it an hour or more each day, compared to only 6.4% of those who used it in the last month but not the last week. Now, imagine that LAST WEEK you did not have access to Generative AI. How many additional hours of work would you have needed to complete the same amount of work? [For X we fill in the respondent’s reported hours worked last week.] The answer options were: Less than 1 hour, 1 hour, 2 hours, 3 hours, 4 hours, More than 4 hours. For respondents who selected “less than 1 hour”, we assume that genAI saved zero hours of work. For respondents who selected “more than 4 hours,” we assume that genAI saved 4 hours of work. These assumptions are conservative in the sense that they reflect a lower bound of time savings. Figure 9 reports the results: 34.2% said genAI saved them an hour or less last week, 25.4% reported two hours, 19.9% reported three hours, and 20.4% reported four hours or more. Among workers who used genAI every day last week, 36.8% reported saving four hours or more, compared to 10.4% of respondents who used it one day last week. We find an average time savings of 5.2% of work hours by genAI users in the November 2024 wave, or about 2.1 hours for a 40-weekly-hour worker. 6 Conclusion Predictions about genAI’s economic impact vary widely, driven by uncertainty over the share of work it can assist and the size of its productivity potential. This paper presents evidence from the first nationally representative U.S. surveys on generative AI use at work and home. We find that a substantial share of individuals already use genAI. Thus far, the pace of overall adoption is rapid compared with past ICT technologies. At work, genAI adoption has followed a similar pace to PCs and is far ahead of genAI adoption by firms. We document wide variation in genAI use across demographic groups and occupations, and provide evidence that both task composition and firm policies appear to play an important role in workers’ adoption choices. Although the intensity of genAI use varies widely, genAI already assists a noticeable share of total work hours, suggesting the potential for meaningful productivity gains. Our findings help lay the groundwork for understanding the labor market implications of genAI. They can also inform responses by managers and policymakers along several dimensions, such as data center and electricity needs, workforce training, and competitive dynamics. References Abbate, J. A.2.1 Weighting Adjustment Based on Awareness In addition to the raking procedure described above to ensure representativeness along de- mographic characteristics, our weighting scheme incorporates results from a new experimental survey that tested alternative question sequences for measuring genAI awareness and use. This experiment revealed that our original question sequence likely underestimated genAI awareness. In response, we applied a reweighting adjustment to our 2024 survey waves to align them with the higher awareness rates observed under the alternative design. This raises reported usage levels modestly (by about 5–6 percentage points) without altering any qualitative patterns in the results. Details. In survey waves prior to August 2025, respondents were first asked whether they had heard of generative AI and, conditional on having heard of it, about their usage. To assess whether this structure induced systematic differences in reporting, we introduced a randomized experiment in a survey conducted in August 2025. Respondents were randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group 1 received the original sequential flow, where they were first asked whether they had heard of genAI, and then whether they used it. Alternatively, Group 2 was first asked whether they used genAI, and if they did not use it they were asked why, with one option being that they had not heard of it. Measurement differences across groups. We found that a larger share of respondents reported having heard of genAI in Group 2. Specifically, 79.6 percent of Group 1 reported having heard of genAI, compared with 88.4 percent of Group 2. Across the two groups, a similar share of respondents reported using genAI conditional on having heard of genAI, suggesting that differential awareness reporting was evenly split between genAI users and non-users. The higher awareness rate in Group 2, combined with similar usage rates conditional on awareness between Groups 1 and 2, translated into higher overall usage rates in Group 2. Similar patterns held across employment status and for usage at home and at work. These results indicate that the initial awareness question (for Group 1) generated a downward bias in reported usage rates. One possible explanation for this pattern is that some respondents strategically reported that they had not heard of genAI because they guessed they would receive fewer questions with that answer. 5

Reweighting strategy. In the August 2025 wave, we can adjust for this bias by reweight- ing Group 1 respondents to match Group 2 usage rates. We constructed adjustment weights across gender, age, education, employment status, and usage (at work and at home) using a raking algorithm that increases the weight of Group 1 users relative to non-users while leaving Group 2 weights unchanged. To maintain coverage across demographic–usage cells, we did not incorporate intensity of usage into the adjustment. (Alternatively, we find that weighting on intensity of genAI interacted with only one demographic characteristics leads to very similar results.) We then apply this adjustment to the 2024 survey waves used in this paper. Since all respondents in these prior waves received the question sequence of Group 1, we apply the adjustment to all respondents in these waves. Furthermore, the share of respondents stating they have heard of genAI (prior to our weighting adjustment) shows no trend between the surveys prior to the August 2025 survey and is very similar to Group 1 in the August 2025 survey (79.6% in vs. 79.4% in the August 2024 survey. This stability suggests that the bias in August 2025 likely existed consistently across earlier waves as well. C SWAA The Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes (SWAA) is a monthly cross-sectional survey of Americans aged 20 to 64 that has been running since May 2020. In December 2024, we incorporated a subset of our questions on genAI usage into the SWAA. Similar to the RPS, the SWAA is fielded online, though it is conducted by a different commercial survey provider (IncQuery) and targets a sample representative of the U.S. population aged 20–64 by age, sex, income, race, and region. Table C.1 shows the analogue of Table A.1 and compares the unweighted SWAA to the weighted CPS. In addition to the targeted variables by the SWAA, we also include live-in-partner (in lieu of marital status) and the number of children. Individual income in the last 12 months is not collected by the SWAA. Similar to the RPS, the SWAA matches the targeted (and non-targeted) quotas fairly closely and the unemployed are somewhat overrepresented. We note that the SWAA uses a single question to determine employment status, which differs from the more detailed protocol used in the CPS and RPS, and map the SWAA’s employment categories into the CPS definitions.2 C.1 Weights To maximize comparability between the RPS and SWAA, we construct our own set of weights rather than using the weights provided by the SWAA.3 In particular, we use again the iterative proportional fitting (raking) algorithm of Deming and Stephan (1940). We include all the demographic variables shown in Table C.1 and also interact all of them with gender. The sampling weights further replicate the employed-at-work rate, the employment rate, and the labor force participation rate in the aggregate and interacted with the demographic variables used for overall weighting. To ensure a sufficient sample size for these latter interactions, we use a broader group for age (20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-64) and a dummy variable for whether there is a child in the house. We also include the broad occupation groups in our weighting scheme, and as for the RPS, without any interaction. D Details on Time Savings and Productivity Calculations D.1 Derivations Using the Aggregate Production Model The Aggregate Productivity Gain from Generative AI We model the economy’s aggregate output using a Cobb-Douglas aggregate production function where labor supply is perfectly substitutable across workers.
